Against all odds, writer Aaron Sorkin and director Bartlett Sher have succeeded in crafting a stage-worthy adaptation of Harper Lee's classic American novel "To Kill a Mockingbird."
If you can put these concerns aside, this Mockingbird is a superbly entertaining and handsomely acted event.
Evidence shows that it does not deface the Harper Lee novel on which it is based, as the Lee estate at one point contended.
The result is a gripping, deeply moving piece of theatre.
If Sorkin's adaptation lacks the subtlety and plainspokenness of Lee's novel, it has moments of old-fashioned power and others of surprising tenderness.
As it is, this version of “To Kill a Mockingbird” is a refreshingly old-fashioned yarn — this is meant in a good way — but lovers of the book will miss its idiosyncratic tone.
Sorkin has written a new play, and it’s characteristically taut and nimble, fluid and funny, with plenty to meditate on and argue about.

The kindness and grace of a man who genuinely believes there is goodness in every man is still a lesson worth heeding by people of any age, especially in a harrowing world like the one we now inhabit.
Aaron Sorkin's adaptation of Harper Lee's novel is a well-meaning but fundamentally misguided attempt to update a classic for our times.

By acknowledging that need in a straightforward, utterly unpretentious manner, accompanied by blazing artistry, Sorkin, Sher and their cast and collaborators have given us a production that feels as urgent and eternal as its source.
This stage Mockingbird is majestically triumphant.
A Mockingbird is a great American story, and this production at the Shubert Theater in Manhattan is a great work of American theater.

In any event, 'To Kill a Mockingbird' (which also sports a period score penned by Tony winner Adam Guettel and played live on organ and guitar) proves to be an engrossing, provocative and uniformly well-acted adaptation - and a fitting addition to a shifting Broadway landscape where an increasing number of plays (including 'Harry Potter and the ...
Even with all its added Sorkinisms, there’s still something firmly classic about Mockingbird; it’s essentially a white-savior story where the savior fails, as nobly as he can.

Where Sorkin succeeds is in getting us to rethink an American classic without any fussiness or archness. Director Bartlett Sher, who's best known for his Tony-winning work on big musicals like 'South Pacific' and 'My Fair Lady,' strikes the right balance between the epic and the intimate.
Then again, we don’t need music: “To Kill a Mockingbird” already sings its own sad song.
If there's one worse thing you can do to a classic than totally reimagine it, it's to tinker with it.
The resulting production, however, makes this reviewer wish the estate had not compromised.
It’s a very good, not great, show.

cn.t: Sorkin's controversial adaptation divides critics but largely succeeds, delivering a timely, well-acted legal thriller. Daniels impresses as Atticus, though purists debate changes to Lee's beloved novel.

vs.sum: The Shubert Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, though some seats may require leaning forward for a full view. The sound quality is generally consistent and clear. While legroom is limited in some areas, the theater's historic charm and central location add to its appeal. Facilities are average, with typical lines at restrooms and concessions.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No wheelchair-accessible restrooms (available across street).
